etymology: From the Latin capitalis (of the head, affecting life), from caput (head); the lawful putting to death of a criminal by the civil magistrate for capital crime.
biblical_def: Capital punishment is the lawful execution of a criminal by the civil magistrate for capital crime, an authority the dictionary holds to be ordained of God, grounded in creation and confirmed under the New Testament. Its foundation is laid before the law of Moses, in the covenant with Noah: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.” The reason given is weighty: murder is so grave precisely because man bears the image of God, and the shedding of innocent blood demands the highest sanction. The Mosaic law confirmed it for murder and other crimes—“He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death”—and forbade ransom for the life of a murderer. The New Testament does not abolish the sword of the magistrate but affirms it: the ruler is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil, and he beareth not the sword in vain. The dictionary distinguishes this lawful, public, judicial taking of life from private vengeance, which Scripture forbids, and from murder, which it condemns. It is committed to the magistrate, not the individual, and is to be exercised with just process and true witness. Against the modern abolitionist sentiment that calls all taking of life equally wrong, the dictionary holds that the magistrate's sword is a divine institution for the restraint of evil and the vindication of the image of God in the murdered; and against the bloodthirsty spirit, it insists the sword be wielded justly, soberly, and only by lawful authority.
webster_summary: The lawful execution of a criminal by the civil magistrate for capital crime; grounded in the covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:6) and confirmed by the magistrate's sword (Romans 13:4), distinct from private vengeance and from murder.
webster_full: CAPITAL PUNISHMENT, noun phrase. [Latin capitalis, affecting the head or life.] The lawful putting to death of a criminal by the magistrate.
Grounded before the law: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed” (Genesis 9:6).
The reason is the image of God in man, which murder violates.
Confirmed in the New Testament: the magistrate beareth not the sword in vain (Romans 13:4).
Committed to the magistrate, not the individual; distinct from private vengeance and murder.
scriptures: Ge 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death.
Moreover ye shall take no satisfaction for the life of a murderer, which is guilty of death: but he shall be surely put to death.
corruption_summary: The abolitionist sentiment calls all taking of life equally wrong, erasing the distinction between murder and lawful execution; the opposite error makes the sword an instrument of cruelty or private revenge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but it meets a live moral confusion. A wide modern sentiment, often draping itself in the language of the sanctity of life, holds that all taking of human life is equally wrong, so that the execution of a murderer is morally indistinguishable from his crime. The dictionary rejects this on the very ground of the sanctity of life: it is because man bears the image of God that the deliberate shedding of innocent blood demands the highest sanction, and God Himself committed the sword to the magistrate for that end. To abolish the distinction between murder and lawful judicial execution is not to honour life but to cheapen the blood of the murdered.

The opposite corruption turns the sword into an instrument of cruelty, hasty judgment, or private revenge. Scripture guards against this with equal care: the death penalty is committed to the magistrate, not the individual; it requires the witness of two or three, never one; and it forbids the shedding of innocent blood, which defiles the land. The dictionary holds the biblical balance: capital punishment is a divine institution for the restraint of evil and the vindication of God's image, to be exercised soberly, justly, and only by lawful authority under due process, never in the spirit of malice or vengeance.
roots_summary: From the Latin caput (head) and capitalis (affecting life or the head); the “sword” (Greek machaira) of Romans 13:4 names the magistrate's lawful power over life.
roots_lines: Capitalis, Latin, “of the head,” hence a crime or penalty affecting life itself.
Machaira, Greek, the sword borne by the magistrate as God's minister (Romans 13:4).
“The image of God” (Genesis 9:6) grounds the gravity of murder and its sanction.
The Noahic covenant predates the Mosaic law, giving the institution creational breadth.
“Take no satisfaction” (Numbers 35:31) forbids ransom for a murderer's life.
usage: The teacher grounded capital punishment in the image of God, the very reason murder is so grave.
He distinguished the magistrate's lawful sword from private vengeance, which Scripture forbids.
She saw that the sword must be wielded justly, with true witness and due process, never in malice.

etymology: From the Latin vindicare (to lay claim, avenge), through Old French vengeance; the just recompense of evil, which Scripture reserves to God and forbids to the individual.
biblical_def: Vengeance, in the biblical sense, is the just recompense of evil, a prerogative Scripture reserves to God and forbids to the private individual. The Lord declares it His own: “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence”; and the apostle, citing this, commands believers, “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” The psalmist appeals to Him as the God to whom vengeance belongeth, and the writer to the Hebrews warns of falling into the hands of the God who has said, “Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense.” The dictionary holds two truths together that the modern mind struggles to keep. First, vengeance is real and righteous: God is just, He will by no means clear the guilty, and He will repay every wrong, either at the cross where the wrath fell on Christ for His people, or in the judgment where it falls on the impenitent. The cry of the martyrs under the altar, “How long, O Lord… dost thou not avenge our blood?” is heard and answered. Second, vengeance is God's, not ours: the believer is forbidden to repay evil for evil, commanded to love his enemies, and called to commit his cause to the righteous Judge. The dictionary marks the doctrine against the sentimentalism that denies God any vengeance at all, emptying His justice, and against the carnal heart that seizes vengeance for itself. To leave vengeance to God is not weakness but faith—the confidence that the Judge of all the earth will do right.
webster_summary: The just recompense of evil, a prerogative God reserves to Himself and forbids to the individual (Romans 12:19; Deuteronomy 32:35); real and righteous in God, forbidden as private revenge to men, who must commit their cause to the righteous Judge.
webster_full: VENGEANCE, noun. [Latin vindicare, to avenge.] The just recompense of evil, belonging to God.
“To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence” (Deuteronomy 32:35).
“Avenge not yourselves… Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Romans 12:19).
Real and righteous: God will repay every wrong, at the cross or in the judgment.
Forbidden to the individual, who must commit his cause to the righteous Judge.
scriptures: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
For we know him that hath said, Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense, saith the Lord. And again, The Lord shall judge his people.
O LORD God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself.
corruption_summary: Sentimentalism denies God any vengeance at all, emptying His justice; the carnal heart seizes vengeance for itself, against the command to leave it to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentimental theology of the age cannot abide a God who avenges, and so it denies Him vengeance altogether, leaving a deity of indulgence who never repays evil. The dictionary names this a corruption of the divine justice. Scripture is emphatic: vengeance belongs to the LORD, who will repay; the same love that gave His Son to bear wrath for His people will pour out wrath on the impenitent who trample that Son under foot. A God incapable of vengeance is a God incapable of justice, and the blood of the martyrs cries to Him in vain. The doctrine of God's vengeance is the comfort of the oppressed and the terror of the oppressor.

The opposite corruption is as old as Cain: the carnal heart that seizes vengeance for itself, repaying evil for evil, nursing its grudges, and calling its retaliation justice. Against this Scripture is equally emphatic: avenge not yourselves; love your enemies; bless them that curse you; give place unto wrath. The dictionary holds the two truths together—that vengeance is real and righteous in God, and forbidden as a private possession to men. To renounce personal revenge is not to deny that justice will be done, but to entrust it to the One who alone can do it without sin: the righteous Judge who will by no means clear the guilty.
roots_summary: From the Latin vindicare (to lay claim, to avenge); the Hebrew naqam (to avenge) and the Greek ekdikesis (vengeance, vindication) name the recompense that belongs to God.
roots_lines: Naqam, Hebrew, to avenge or take vengeance, the LORD's prerogative.
Ekdikesis, Greek, vengeance or vindication, “vengeance is mine” (Romans 12:19).
Vindicare, Latin, to lay legal claim, to avenge, the root of “vengeance” and “vindicate.”
“Give place unto wrath” commits the matter to the wrath of God, not the hand of man.
The cry “how long… dost thou not avenge?” (Revelation 6:10) shows vengeance is heard and answered.
usage: The pastor comforted the wronged that vengeance belongs to the LORD, who will repay in His time.
He rebuked the brother nursing revenge, for Scripture forbids us to avenge ourselves.
She gave place unto wrath, entrusting her cause to the righteous Judge who cannot err.

etymology: From the Latin persequi (to pursue, to hunt down); the affliction and pursuit of the people of God for righteousness' and Christ's sake.
biblical_def: Persecution is the affliction, pursuit, and hostility that the people of God suffer for righteousness' sake and for the name of Christ. The Lord pronounced it a beatitude, not a misfortune: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He warned His disciples plainly: “The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you.” The apostle states it as a rule, not an exception: “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.” The dictionary holds persecution to be the ordinary lot of the faithful church in a fallen and hostile world, not a sign of God's displeasure but often of His favour, for the world hated the Master first. It takes many forms—mockery, slander, exclusion, loss of livelihood, imprisonment, and death—and the church's history is written in the blood of the martyrs, the seed of the church. Yet the Lord's command to the persecuted is not retaliation but love: “Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” The dictionary marks two errors. The prosperity gospel promises the believer ease and freedom from suffering, contradicting the apostle's plain word that the godly shall be persecuted. And the spirit of self-pity or vengeance would have the persecuted curse their persecutors, when Christ commands them to bless. True persecution, borne in the spirit of Christ, is a participation in His sufferings and a pledge of His glory.
webster_summary: The affliction the people of God suffer for righteousness and the name of Christ; pronounced a beatitude (Matthew 5:10) and the ordinary lot of the godly (2 Timothy 3:12), met not with retaliation but with love of enemies.
webster_full: PERSECUTION, noun. [Latin persequi, to pursue or hunt down.] Affliction suffered for righteousness and for Christ.
“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Matthew 5:10).
“All that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12).
The servant is not greater than his Lord; they persecuted Him first (John 15:20).
Met not with retaliation but with love of enemies and prayer for persecutors (Matthew 5:44).
scriptures: Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel promises freedom from suffering, against the apostle's plain word; the spirit of self-pity or vengeance would curse the persecutor, when Christ commands the persecuted to bless.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel and the broader comfort-Christianity of the age promise the believer health, ease, and the favour of the world, treating suffering as a defect of faith. This directly contradicts the apostle: all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. The dictionary names the false promise: the Lord did not exempt His servants from the hatred that fell on Him but forewarned them of it and called it blessed. A Christianity that has made peace with the world and suffers nothing for righteousness should examine whether it is following the crucified Christ at all.

A second corruption arises within the persecuted themselves: the temptation to self-pity, bitterness, or vengeance against their persecutors. But the Lord's command turns the whole disposition upside down: love your enemies, bless them that curse you, pray for them which persecute you. The blood of the martyrs was sown not in curses but in prayers—Stephen prayed for his murderers as Christ prayed for His. The dictionary recovers the doctrine: persecution is the ordinary lot of the faithful, a sharing in Christ's sufferings and a pledge of His kingdom, to be borne not with retaliation but with the patient, forgiving love of the Master who endured the cross before His servants.
roots_summary: From the Latin persequi (to pursue, hunt down); the Greek dioko (to pursue, persecute) is the same verb used for “pressing toward the mark,” the world pursuing the saints as the saint pursues Christ.
roots_lines: Persequi, Latin, to pursue or hunt down, the root of “persecution.”
Dioko, Greek, to pursue or persecute, also “to press toward” a goal.
Thlipsis, Greek, tribulation or pressing affliction, often joined to persecution.
Martys, Greek, a witness, whence “martyr,” the persecuted unto death.
“The servant is not greater than his lord” sets the pattern of Christ before the church.
usage: The pastor warned the comfortable church that all who live godly shall suffer persecution.
He taught the persecuted to bless and not curse, as Stephen prayed for those who stoned him.
She counted it a beatitude to be reproached for Christ, for so men treated the prophets before her.

etymology: From “reckoning,” an accounting or settling of accounts; the appointed day on which every man shall give account of himself to God.
biblical_def: The day of reckoning is the appointed day on which every man shall give account of himself to God, when the books are opened and the secrets of all hearts are judged. Scripture sets the certainty of it as a fixed appointment: “It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.” The reckoning is universal and personal: “every one of us shall give account of himself to God,” and “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body… whether it be good or bad.” The Lord warns that the reckoning reaches even to words: “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.” The dictionary holds the day of reckoning as a sure and solemn doctrine, the answer of God's justice to a world that seems to let sin go unpunished and righteousness unrewarded. Nothing is forgotten, nothing overlooked; the Judge of all the earth will do right. For the impenitent, the reckoning is terror, for it issues in eternal condemnation; for the believer, it holds no condemnation, for Christ has borne his judgment, yet his works shall be tried, and he shall receive his reward of grace. The dictionary marks the doctrine against the practical atheism that lives as though no account will ever be given, and against the universalism that empties the reckoning of all consequence by saving all in the end. The day of reckoning is real, certain, particular, and final; it is the great motive to sober watchfulness and the great comfort of the wronged.
webster_summary: The appointed day on which every man shall give account of himself to God (Romans 14:12; Hebrews 9:27), reaching even to idle words; terror to the impenitent, the trying of works to the believer, the answer of God's justice to a sinful world.
webster_full: DAY OF RECKONING, noun phrase. The appointed day of account before God, when the secrets of all hearts are judged.
“It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Hebrews 9:27).
“Every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12).
The reckoning reaches even to every idle word (Matthew 12:36).
Terror to the impenitent; the trying of works, with no condemnation, to the believer.
scriptures: But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
corruption_summary: Practical atheism lives as though no account will ever be given, while universalism empties the reckoning of consequence by saving all in the end; both deny the certainty and finality of the day.
corruption_paragraphs: The practical atheism of the age lives as though there will be no reckoning—as though death were the end, or God indifferent to how men live. The dictionary answers with the fixed appointment of Scripture: it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment. The seeming impunity of the wicked and the unrewarded labour of the righteous are not the last word; there is a day when every account is settled, every idle word weighed, and every secret thing brought into judgment. To forget the reckoning is to live a lie; to remember it is the beginning of sober wisdom.

The opposite corruption is the universalism that admits a judgment but empties it of consequence, holding that all will be saved in the end and the reckoning issues in no eternal loss. Scripture forbids this conclusion: the Judge will say to some, Depart from me; the impenitent face eternal condemnation, not a temporary chastening that ends in glory for all. The dictionary holds the reckoning to be real, particular, and final—terror to the impenitent and the trying of works to the believer, whose sins were judged already at the cross. The day of reckoning is the answer of God's justice and the great motive to watchfulness, repentance, and faith.
roots_summary: From “reckoning,” a settling of accounts; the Greek logos (account, word) in “give account” (logon apodidomi) names the rendering of a final reckoning to God.
roots_lines: Logon apodidomi, Greek, “to render an account,” the verb of the reckoning.
“Reckoning,” an accounting or settling, as of a steward's books.
Bema, Greek, the judgment seat before which all must appear (2 Corinthians 5:10).
“Appointed” (Greek apokeitai) marks the judgment as a fixed and certain decree.
“Every idle word” (Matthew 12:36) shows the reckoning's searching reach.
usage: The preacher set the day of reckoning before the careless, that they might give account with joy and not with grief.
He warned that even idle words shall be reckoned, and called his hearers to sober speech.
She lived in view of the judgment seat, knowing every one must give account of himself to God.

etymology: From the prophetic figure that likens idolatry and worldliness to marital infidelity; God the husband of His covenant people, who play the harlot when they forsake Him.
biblical_def: Spiritual adultery is the unfaithfulness of God's covenant people when they forsake Him for other lovers—idols, false gods, or the world—a sin Scripture portrays under the figure of marital infidelity. The LORD is the husband of His people; Israel is the wife of His covenant; and her idolatry is adultery against Him. So the prophets cry: “Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel”; and Ezekiel laments the wife that committeth adultery, taking strangers instead of her husband. Hosea was commanded to take a wife of whoredoms as a living parable of the land that had committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD. The New Testament carries the figure to the heart: “Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God.” The dictionary marks spiritual adultery as a sin of the affections, not merely of outward act: it is the heart that loves and trusts and serves another in the place that belongs to God alone. Every idol, whether of wood or of the heart—money, pleasure, reputation, self—is a rival lover, and to embrace it is to break covenant with the divine Husband. The doctrine deepens the seriousness of idolatry and worldliness by setting them in the language of betrayed love; and it magnifies the grace of God, who, like Hosea redeeming his faithless wife, woos back His adulterous people and says, I will betroth thee unto me for ever.
webster_summary: The unfaithfulness of God's covenant people when they forsake Him for idols or the world (Jeremiah 3:20; James 4:4); idolatry and worldliness portrayed as marital infidelity against the divine Husband, a sin of the affections, not merely of act.
webster_full: SPIRITUAL ADULTERY, noun phrase. Unfaithfulness to God, who is the husband of His covenant people, by turning to idols or the world.
Israel deals treacherously with the LORD as a wife departing from her husband (Jeremiah 3:20).
Hosea's marriage figures the land that committed whoredom, departing from the LORD (Hosea 1:2).
“The friendship of the world is enmity with God” (James 4:4).
A sin of the affections: loving, trusting, or serving another in God's place.
scriptures: Jas 4:4
Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God.
Jer 3:20
Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD.
But as a wife that committeth adultery, which taketh strangers instead of her husband!
Ho 1:2

The beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea. And the LORD said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the trivializing of idolatry and worldliness, so that the believer's flirtation with the world is no longer felt as betrayal of a covenant Husband.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gravity of worldliness as covenant infidelity. The modern believer easily regards friendship with the world as harmless and idolatry as a primitive sin of statues, feeling no betrayal in loving money, pleasure, or self. The prophets and the apostle James forbid this complacency: to befriend the world is to commit adultery against God, who is the Husband of His people. The figure of marital betrayal restores the seriousness; the heart that gives to a rival what belongs to God alone has broken covenant with its Lord.

The doctrine also magnifies the astonishing grace of God toward His unfaithful people. Hosea was commanded to redeem his adulterous wife, a living parable of the LORD who pursues His faithless bride, betroths her again unto Himself in righteousness, and heals her backsliding. The dictionary holds both edges: spiritual adultery is real betrayal, to be repented of with shame; and the divine Husband is full of mercy, calling His wandering people home. The remedy is not lighter views of the sin but a heart wholly restored to its first love, that the believer cleave to the Lord and renounce every rival lover.
roots_summary: From the prophetic marriage-figure: God the husband, His people the wife, and idolatry the zenunim (whoredoms) of an unfaithful spouse; the Greek moichalis (adulteress) is James's word for the worldly church.
roots_lines: Zanah, Hebrew, to commit fornication or play the harlot, used of Israel's idolatry.
Zenunim, Hebrew, “whoredoms,” the prophetic term for covenant unfaithfulness.
Moichalis, Greek, an adulteress, James's address to the world-loving church.
The marriage-covenant figure casts the LORD as husband and His people as wife.
Hosea's marriage enacts the parable of God's faithless yet redeemed bride.
usage: The pastor named the love of the world as spiritual adultery, a betrayal of the covenant Husband.
He preached Hosea to show the grace that redeems even an adulterous bride.
She repented of the idols of her heart, seeing them as rival lovers against her Lord.

pos: noun phrase (the authorship of the Pentateuch)
etymology: From “Mosaic” (of Moses) and “authorship”; the doctrine that Moses, under divine inspiration, is the author of the Pentateuch, the first five books of Scripture.
biblical_def: Mosaic authorship is the doctrine, held by the dictionary as the historic faith of the church and the testimony of Scripture itself, that Moses, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, is the author of the Pentateuch—Genesis through Deuteronomy, the books called “the law of Moses.” The Scriptures attest it within themselves: “Moses wrote all the words of the LORD”; and when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, he commanded its keeping beside the ark. The Lord Jesus confirmed it, speaking of “the book of Moses” and asking, “Did not Moses give you the law?”; He grounded an argument for the resurrection on what God said to Moses in the bush, and declared that Moses wrote of Him. The apostles likewise ascribe the law to Moses throughout. The dictionary acknowledges that the death of Moses (Deuteronomy 34) and a few editorial notes were added by a later inspired hand, as the church has long recognized, without overturning the substantial Mosaic authorship of the whole. Against this stands the documentary hypothesis (the JEDP theory of Wellhausen and his successors), which fragments the Pentateuch into supposed sources—Yahwist, Elohist, Deuteronomist, Priestly—woven together by post-exilic redactors centuries after Moses, denying his authorship altogether. The dictionary rejects the documentary hypothesis as a critical construction resting on naturalistic assumptions, contradicting the witness of Christ and the Scriptures, and dissolving the historical foundation of the faith. To deny that Moses wrote the law is, in the end, to call the Lord Jesus mistaken; the dictionary holds with Him that Moses wrote, and that he wrote of Christ.
webster_summary: The doctrine that Moses, under inspiration, authored the Pentateuch, attested by Scripture and confirmed by Christ (John 7:19; Mark 12:26); against the documentary hypothesis (JEDP), which fragments the law into late sources and denies Mosaic authorship.
webster_full: MOSAIC AUTHORSHIP, noun phrase. The doctrine that Moses, under inspiration, authored the Pentateuch.
“Moses wrote all the words of the LORD” (Exodus 24:4).
Confirmed by Christ, who spoke of “the book of Moses” and said Moses gave the law (Mark 12:26; John 7:19).
A few editorial notes (as Moses' death, Deuteronomy 34) were added by a later inspired hand.
Against the documentary hypothesis (JEDP), which denies Mosaic authorship on naturalistic grounds.
scriptures: And Moses wrote all the words of the LORD, and rose up early in the morning, and builded an altar under the hill, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel.
And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished,
And as touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?
Joh 7:19
Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keepeth the law? Why go ye about to kill me?
corruption_summary: The documentary hypothesis (JEDP) fragments the Pentateuch into late, competing sources stitched together by post-exilic redactors, denying Mosaic authorship and contradicting the testimony of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The documentary hypothesis, given its classic form by Julius Wellhausen, divides the Pentateuch among four supposed sources—the Yahwist (J), Elohist (E), Deuteronomist (D), and Priestly (P)—composed over centuries and combined by redactors long after Moses, often centuries after the exile. The dictionary names this a corruption of the doctrine of Scripture. It rests on naturalistic premises that exclude prophecy and inspiration, treats divine names and stylistic variety as marks of separate authors rather than the richness of one, and reconstructs Israel's religion on an evolutionary scheme foreign to the text. Above all, it contradicts the Lord Jesus, who repeatedly ascribed the law to Moses and said Moses wrote of Him.

The dictionary affirms substantial Mosaic authorship while acknowledging, as the church always has, that a later inspired hand recorded Moses' death and inserted a few explanatory notes—an editorial reality wholly different from the wholesale dismemberment the critics propose. To grant a few post-Mosaic glosses is not to concede the documentary hypothesis but to read the text honestly. The stakes are not academic: the historicity of the law, the integrity of the canon, and the trustworthiness of Christ's own testimony stand together. The dictionary holds that Moses wrote the law of God, and that the One greater than Moses confirmed it.
roots_summary: From “Mosaic” (pertaining to Moses, Hebrew Mosheh) and “authorship”; the phrase “the book of Moses” (Greek biblos Mouseos) names the Pentateuch by its author.
roots_lines: Mosheh, Hebrew, Moses, “drawn out” of the water, the lawgiver and prophet.
“The law of Moses” (Hebrew torat Mosheh) names the Pentateuch by its author.
“The book of Moses” (Greek biblos Mouseos) is the Lord's own phrase (Mark 12:26).
JEDP, the four hypothetical sources of the documentary theory, rejected by the dictionary.
“Wellhausen,” the nineteenth-century critic whose scheme gave the hypothesis its classic shape.
usage: The teacher defended Mosaic authorship from the testimony of Christ, who said Moses wrote of Him.
He showed that divine names and varied style mark the richness of one author, not the seams of four.
She granted the note of Moses' death as a later inspired addition, without conceding the JEDP scheme.

etymology: From the recurring biblical theme of the wilderness as the place of God's proving of His people; Israel's forty years and Christ's forty days the chief instances.
biblical_def: The wilderness tests are the trials by which God proves His people in the desert, the place He appoints for humbling, sifting, and the manifesting of what is in the heart. Of Israel's forty years Moses said, “Thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.” The wilderness was no accident of geography but a school of faith, where God fed them with manna, gave water from the rock, and tested whether they would trust and obey. Israel largely failed—murmuring, lusting, tempting God, and falling in the day of provocation—and these things, the apostle says, were written for our admonition, that we sin not as they sinned. Where the first Israel failed, the true Israel triumphed: the Lord Jesus was led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil, and where Adam fell in a garden of plenty and Israel fell in the desert of want, Christ overcame, answering every temptation with the written Word, “It is written.” The dictionary marks the wilderness tests as a pattern of the Christian life: God leads His people through seasons of want and trial, not to destroy but to humble and prove them, that they may learn to live by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God. The proper response is not the murmuring of unbelief but the trust that knows the same God who led into the wilderness will lead through it, having Himself, in Christ, passed the test His people failed.
webster_summary: The trials by which God proves His people in the desert (Deuteronomy 8:2); Israel's forty years and Christ's forty days the chief instances—where the first Israel murmured and fell, the true Israel overcame by the written Word.
webster_full: WILDERNESS TESTS, noun phrase. The trials by which God proves His people in the desert, to humble and to manifest the heart.
Israel's forty years were to humble and prove them, to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2).
They largely failed—murmuring, lusting, and provoking God in the day of temptation.
These things were written for our admonition (1 Corinthians 10:11).
Christ, the true Israel, overcame in the wilderness by the written Word (Matthew 4:1).
scriptures: De 8:2

Mt 4:1
Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil.
Heb 3:8
Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the prosperity gospel that denies God leads His people through seasons of want, and the murmuring heart that reads trial as God's rejection.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints seasons of trial to humble and prove His people. The prosperity gospel teaches that the favour of God means continual plenty and ease, so that the wilderness—want, hunger, hardship—must be a sign of insufficient faith or hidden sin. But God Himself led Israel into the wilderness to humble and to prove them, and led His own Son there to be tempted. The desert is not the mark of God's absence but often the school of His nearest dealing.

The opposite corruption is the murmuring of unbelief, which reads every trial as God's rejection and turns, like Israel, to complaint and the longing for Egypt. The apostle warns that these things were written for our admonition. The dictionary recovers the wilderness tests as a pattern of sanctification: God leads His people through want to teach them to live by every word of His mouth, and the believer's part is not to murmur but to trust—remembering that the Lord Jesus, the true Israel, passed in the desert the very test His people failed, and now leads them through their own wilderness as a faithful Captain who knows the way.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew midbar (wilderness, desert) and nasah (to test, prove); the forty years and forty days mark the wilderness as God's appointed place of proving.
roots_lines: Midbar, Hebrew, wilderness or desert, the place of God's proving of Israel.
Nasah, Hebrew, to test, try, or prove, as God proved Israel's heart.
Massah and Meribah, the “temptation” and “strife” where Israel provoked God.
The forty years of Israel answer the forty days of Christ's temptation.
“It is written” (Greek gegraptai) is the Lord's threefold answer to the tempter.
usage: The pastor preached the wilderness tests to comfort the suffering, for God leads His own through want to prove them.
He warned against the murmuring of Israel, written for our admonition that we trust and not complain.
She saw that Christ overcame in the desert where Israel fell, and followed her Captain through the trial.

etymology: From the account in Acts 10 of the sheet let down from heaven; the vision by which God prepared Peter to carry the gospel to the Gentiles.
biblical_def: Peter's vision is the revelation given to the apostle on the housetop at Joppa, recorded in Acts 10, by which God prepared him to receive the Gentiles into the church. As Peter prayed and grew hungry, he saw heaven opened and a great sheet let down, full of all manner of beasts, creeping things, and fowls, clean and unclean together; and a voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” When Peter refused, having never eaten anything common or unclean, the voice answered, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common,” and this was done three times. While Peter doubted what it meant, the messengers of Cornelius the Roman centurion arrived, and the Spirit bade him go with them. Peter perceived the meaning: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean,” and standing in the house of a Gentile he confessed, “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons.” The dictionary holds Peter's vision to teach two truths. First, the abolition of the old ceremonial distinction between clean and unclean foods, fulfilled and set aside in Christ, who declared all meats clean. Second, and chiefly, the opening of the gospel to the Gentiles: the dividing wall is broken down, and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. The dictionary marks the vision against the error that would read it as a charter for moral indifference or the abolition of God's moral law; it abolished the ceremonial shadow and the partition between the nations, not the abiding commands of God. It is a landmark of redemptive history: the household of faith opened to all peoples, that the promise to Abraham might be fulfilled, in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
webster_summary: The vision of the sheet let down from heaven (Acts 10), by which God abolished the clean/unclean ceremonial distinction and, chiefly, opened the gospel to the Gentiles; “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.”
webster_full: PETER'S VISION, noun phrase. The revelation of the sheet let down from heaven at Joppa (Acts 10).
A voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat,” of beasts clean and unclean together.
“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Acts 10:15), spoken thrice.
It abolished the ceremonial distinction of clean and unclean foods, fulfilled in Christ.
Chiefly, it opened the gospel to the Gentiles: God is no respecter of persons (Acts 10:34).
scriptures: And there came a voice to him, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.

And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.
Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is reading the vision as a charter for moral indifference, as though “call nothing unclean” abolished God's moral law along with the ceremonial.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the careful distinction between the ceremonial law, fulfilled and set aside in Christ, and the moral law, which abides. Peter's vision is sometimes pressed into the service of moral license—“God said call nothing unclean,” therefore no behaviour may be named sin. This wrests the text. The vision abolished the dietary distinctions of the ceremonial code and broke down the partition between Jew and Gentile; it said nothing to overturn the moral commands of God, which the apostles everywhere upheld. The clean/unclean of Leviticus is fulfilled in Christ; the “thou shalt not” of the Decalogue is not.

Rightly read, Peter's vision is one of the great landmarks of redemptive history: the gospel goes to the nations, and in Christ the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down. The dictionary holds it as the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham, that in his seed all the families of the earth should be blessed. It teaches that God is no respecter of persons—not that all conduct is acceptable, but that men of every nation who fear God and work righteousness are accepted in Christ. The vision opened the church to the world; it did not open the law of God to revision.
roots_summary: From the account at Joppa: the “sheet” (Greek othone) let down, the “common” (koinos) and “unclean” (akathartos) that God had cleansed (katharizo).
roots_lines: Othone, Greek, a sheet or large linen, let down from heaven in the vision.
Koinos, Greek, “common,” ceremonially defiled, what Peter would not eat.
Akathartos, Greek, unclean, the category abolished for foods in Christ.
Katharizo, Greek, to cleanse, “what God hath cleansed” (Acts 10:15).
“No respecter of persons” (Greek prosopolemptes) names God's impartiality toward the nations.
usage: The teacher showed that Peter's vision abolished the ceremonial law of foods, not the moral law of God.
He preached the breaking of the wall between Jew and Gentile, the gospel opened to all nations.
She rejoiced that God is no respecter of persons, receiving worshippers of every nation in Christ.

etymology: The traditional name for Herod's massacre of the children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16); “innocents” from the Latin innocentes, the guiltless little ones slain.
biblical_def: The slaughter of the innocents is the massacre of the male children of Bethlehem ordered by Herod the Great in his rage to destroy the newborn King. When the wise men did not return to him, Herod, exceeding wroth, sent forth and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time he had inquired of the wise men. The Lord Jesus was preserved, for the angel had warned Joseph to take the young child and His mother and flee into Egypt. Matthew sees in the weeping of Bethlehem the fulfilment of Jeremiah: “In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.” The dictionary holds the account as true history and reads it for its solemn lessons. It displays the murderous enmity of the world against Christ from His very infancy, the same enmity that pursued Him to the cross. It shows the tyrant's readiness to shed innocent blood to guard his throne, a perennial mark of ungodly power. And it sets the cost of redemption against the backdrop of grief: the King came into a world of Herods, and His coming, while it brought salvation, also provoked the rage of hell. The slaughter of the innocents stands as a witness against the shedding of innocent blood in every age, and as a reminder that the Prince of Peace was born into the world's violence, to bear it and at last to end it.
webster_summary: Herod's massacre of the male children of Bethlehem two years old and under, in his rage to destroy the newborn King (Matthew 2:16); the world's enmity against Christ from His infancy, and the fulfilment of Rachel's weeping.
webster_full: SLAUGHTER OF THE INNOCENTS, noun phrase. Herod's massacre of the children of Bethlehem to destroy the newborn Christ.
He slew all the children two years old and under in Bethlehem and its coasts (Matthew 2:16).
The Lord Jesus was preserved by the flight into Egypt (Matthew 2:13).
It fulfilled Jeremiah's “Rachel weeping for her children” (Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18).
It displays the world's murderous enmity against Christ from His infancy.
scriptures: Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men.
In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.
Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.

And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the critical denial of its historicity and the sentimental Christmas that forgets the blood and grief into which the King was born.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the historicity of the account and the gravity of innocent blood. Some critics deny the slaughter ever happened, since no source outside Matthew records it; but the deed is wholly in character with Herod the Great, who murdered his own sons and wife to secure his throne, and the small population of Bethlehem would make the massacre a minor item in a brutal reign. The dictionary affirms the Gospel's witness: the event is true history, and the silence of pagan chroniclers proves nothing against the inspired record.

The sentimental celebration of Christmas, all light and comfort, easily forgets that the King was born into a world of violence and that His coming provoked the rage of a murderous tyrant. The slaughter of the innocents restores the shadow that lies across the manger: the enmity of the world against Christ began at His birth and pursued Him to the cross. The dictionary reads the account as a perpetual witness against the shedding of innocent blood by ungodly power, and as a reminder that the Prince of Peace entered the world's grief and bloodshed in order to bear it, to weep with the weeping, and at last to wipe away every tear.
roots_summary: From “innocents” (Latin innocentes, the guiltless), the traditional name for the slain children of Bethlehem; the “coasts” (Greek horia, borders) mark the region around the town.
roots_lines: Innocentes, Latin, the guiltless, the name given the slaughtered children.
Horia, Greek, “coasts” or borders, the region of Bethlehem affected.
Herod “the Great,” the Idumean king infamous for murdering his own kin.
“Rachel weeping” (Jeremiah 31:15) is the prophetic lament Matthew sees fulfilled.
The “flight into Egypt” preserves the Christ and recalls Israel's own sojourn there.
usage: The pastor set the slaughter of the innocents against the sentimental Christmas, recalling the grief into which Christ was born.
He defended the event as true history, noting it suited Herod's murderous reign exactly.
She heard in Rachel's weeping a witness against the shedding of innocent blood in every age.

etymology: From the parable of Matthew 18; the servant forgiven a vast debt who refused to forgive his fellow a small one, and was delivered to the tormentors.
biblical_def: The unmerciful servant is the figure of our Lord's parable in Matthew 18, told in answer to Peter's question how often he must forgive his brother. A king took account of his servants and found one owing ten thousand talents—an unpayable sum, the wages of many lifetimes—and when the servant could not pay and begged for patience, the king was moved with compassion, loosed him, and forgave him the whole debt. But that same servant went out, found a fellow-servant owing him a hundred pence—a trifling sum—took him by the throat, and cast him into prison till he should pay. When his lord heard of it, he called him: “O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” And he delivered him to the tormentors till he should pay all. The Lord drives the lesson home: “So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.” The dictionary holds the parable to teach that the believer, forgiven an infinite debt by God, is bound to forgive the comparatively trifling wrongs done to him. The unforgiving spirit is not a small fault but the mark of one who has not understood or received the grace he professes; an unforgiven heart toward others betrays a heart that has never truly known forgiveness from God. The dictionary marks the parable against the cheap grace that severs forgiveness from a forgiving life, and against the works-righteousness that would make our forgiving the ground of God's; rather, God's vast mercy is the ground and motive of ours, and the absence of mercy toward others exposes the absence of grace within.
webster_summary: The servant of Christ's parable forgiven an unpayable debt who refused his fellow a trifling one, and was delivered to the tormentors (Matthew 18:32-35); the forgiven who will not forgive betrays a heart that has not received grace.
webster_full: UNMERCIFUL SERVANT, noun phrase. The servant of Matthew 18 forgiven a vast debt who would not forgive a small one.
Told in answer to Peter's question how often he must forgive (Matthew 18:21).
Forgiven ten thousand talents, he jailed a fellow owing a hundred pence.
“Shouldest not thou also have had compassion… even as I had pity on thee?” (Matthew 18:33).
“So likewise shall my heavenly Father do… if ye from your hearts forgive not” (Matthew 18:35).
scriptures: Then his lord, after that he had called him, said unto him, O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me:
Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?
So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.
Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?
corruption_summary: Cheap grace severs forgiveness from a forgiving life, while works-righteousness makes our forgiving the ground of God's; both miss that God's vast mercy is the ground and motive of ours.
corruption_paragraphs: Cheap grace hears the parable's comfort—the unpayable debt forgiven—and ignores its warning, severing God's forgiveness from any forgiving life in the one forgiven. But the Lord makes the unforgiving servant a wicked servant, delivered to the tormentors, and applies it directly: so shall the Father do to those who will not forgive their brethren from the heart. The dictionary names the error: a professed faith that leaves the heart hard and vengeful toward others is exposed by this parable as a faith that has never truly received the grace it claims. The forgiven forgive; the unforgiving show they were never forgiven.

The opposite error reads the parable as works-righteousness, as though our forgiving others earned or caused God's forgiveness of us. The order of the parable forbids this: the king forgave the great debt first, freely, moved with compassion, before any question of the servant's mercy arose. God's prior, vast, unmerited mercy is the ground and the motive of ours; we forgive because we have been forgiven, not in order to be. The dictionary holds the balance: forgiveness is received by grace, not earned by forgiving; and the grace truly received unfailingly produces a forgiving heart, so that the refusal to forgive is the surest sign that grace has not been received at all.
roots_summary: From the parable's contrast of debts: ten thousand “talents” (a vast sum) against a hundred “pence” (Greek denaria, a trifle); the “tormentors” (Greek basanistes) figure the judgment on the unforgiving.
roots_lines: Talanton, Greek, a talent, an enormous sum; ten thousand was beyond all payment.
Denarion, Greek, a penny, a day's wage; a hundred was a trifling debt.
Basanistes, Greek, a tormentor or jailer, to whom the wicked servant was delivered.
“From your hearts” (Greek apo ton kardion) marks true forgiveness as inward, not formal.
Peter's “till seven times” is answered by “until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22).
usage: The pastor preached the unmerciful servant to show that the forgiven must forgive, or prove they were never forgiven.
He warned that an unforgiving heart is no small fault but the mark of grace unreceived.
She forgave the wrong done her, remembering the vast debt her Lord had freely cancelled.
